1
It made sense not to tell her then. By the end, she was a child. By the end, I was a different type of mother. Every day, a new negotiation: Please take a bite of your food for me? Could you swallow your pills? Let the nurse draw your blood? Granny, I’m going to lift you now. Help change your cloths. Your clothes. Rub your legs. Your feet. Tell me where it hurts. If you try, I will give you more Pepsi. More ice cream. If you try, I will—
2
My second date with her was to an in-home art installation. Once upstairs, we were prompted to leave an encouraging note for future guests to see. Across the room, avoiding each other’s eye, we write the same Audre Lorde quote: I am deliberate and afraid of nothing. That was more than two years ago, when we planned to be casual. When our texts went weeks unsent. When both our grandmothers were earthside, not yet pictures on our dressers.
3
I joked with Ajanae once that my Granny crossed over and learned more about me than she bargained for. I’m not sure how that works. Does she peek across the veil and frown when she sees that girl seated on my lap? It no longer matters that I was a coward. That I half hinted once, and never brought it up again. That I brought it up, long after her brain backtracked. I knew she couldn’t remember.
4
That was then. Now, I would confess twenty times a day, if it meant she died knowing who loved me. Granny, while I’m sleeping, she kisses my shoulders. She brought me a tiny jade elephant to remind me of you, in those first months when grief tried to walk off with me, and I almost let it. Granny. I walk into her room, and lying right beside her pillow is the book I dedicated to you.
